title: Tired of thinking? Think again! An experience-sampling study of bidirectional dynamics between rumination and mental fatigue in athletes.
abstract: Recovery days are intended to support psychological and physical recovery, yet repetitive sport-related thinking may interfere with this process. This four-week experience-sampling study examined the dynamic interplay between rumination and mental fatigue during rest days in competitive athletes, as well as the moderating roles of perfectionistic concerns and perfectionistic strivings. A total of 134 athletes completed repeated rest-day assessments of rumination and mental fatigue, with perfectionism measured at baseline using a sport-adapted version of the FMPS-Brief. Continuous-time structural equation modelling revealed significant bidirectional coupling between rumination and mental fatigue, supporting a self-reinforcing dynamic in which rumination fuels fatigue, and accumulated fatigue heightens the likelihood of further rumination, creating a 'vicious cycle'. The rumination → mental fatigue pathway was stronger than the reverse, underscoring the critical importance of mental rest and psychological recovery in sport. Perfectionistic concerns significantly moderated this association, suggesting that athletes high in evaluative self-criticism may be more vulnerable to the rumination-fatigue cycle, whereas perfectionistic strivings did not exert a moderating effect. These findings advance a process-oriented understanding of psychological recovery in athletes and may inform future research on how short-term rumination-fatigue dynamics contribute to longer-term maladaptive recovery patterns, including burnout risk. Interventions targeting repetitive negative thinking, such as mindfulness-, cognitive-behavioral-, or acceptance-based approaches, may help athletes preserve psychological recovery under performance demands.
